Ch06 Lab Principal Components Regression

Bruce Hartman

University of St. Francis

2025-08-18 Revised 2026-10-16T13:02:19

Abstract

We use principal components analysis (PCA) to reduce the dimension (number of drivers) we need to consider in a problem. PCA replaces the driers with linear combinations of them; we may need only a few components to achieve substantially all the value of the original drivers.

Introduction

This section follows Michy (2016). Principal Components Regression (PCR) or Principal Components Analysis (PCA) is one method of reducing the dimension of a problem. If there are so many drivers that regression alone finds it difficult to select the ones to use, perhaps instead we can use some linear combinations of the drivers.

Sometimes this is called ‘feature selection’. A feature is a new variable concocted from the original ones.

Essentially we come up with a calculation to abstract from the drivers some few features alled ‘components’ that capture as much or all of the capability they have to predict. But the regression on the components will be much simpler. As a bonus, the components themselves might reveal new concepts of how the drivers cluster together. We might even to be able to discern ‘meanings’ for the components. But that isn’t necessary to make the method work. It’s just a bonus if we can from a management perspective identify components with unrevealed abilities the observations have that allow us to analyze them.

Why use it? PCA reduces the dimension (number of drivers) in the data set. See Reference 1 for a discussion of advantages and disadvantages.

One could see dimension reduction as a theme for all of artificial intelligence. Neural networks do the same thing. Here’s how they construct the network. For the first ‘hidden’ layer, a NN figures out how to put weights on the drivers to best fit the target using the new nodes in that layer. We’ve specified how many nodes there will be in every layer. For the second hidden layer, it does the same, using the nodes or features or pseudo-drivers from the previous layer. And so on, for as many hidden layers specified. In the final layer, the target is modeled using the final hidden layer nodes. So you see we have a kind of repeated ‘dimension reduction’. It may not be a reduction, since we could specify an increasing number of nodes in the hidden layers, but normally there are fewer in each layer.

Packages

One can use the pls package for determining the principal components. We are including it. But already in R there is the prcomp package that performs similar analysis.

library(pls) # for PCA
library(factoextra) # for clustering analysis and PCA plotting; 
library(FactoMineR) # for some analytics and graphics
library(ISLR2) # package contains data files
library(mbadtools, quietly = TRUE) # used to manipulate data and plot

Data

We use the Hitters dataset from the ISLR2 package.

data(Hitters)
Hitters=na.omit(Hitters) # remove the NAs
Hitters %>% skim

Linear Regression

Before we start let’s run a simple MLR on these all and see what the results are. The idea of PCA is that fewer variables is better, and 19 driver variables is way too many to comprehend for decision-making.

lm.fit=lm(Salary~.,data=Hitters)
lm.fit %>% glance %>% gt_add_significance()

Only a few variables are significant, and the Adjusted R-squared is .51. There are some outliers to be sure, and scale-location shows rising residuals!! The result is not that desirable. But the residuals are more or less normally distributed.

Principal Components Analysis

Principal Components Analysis tries to simplify the data by projecting the drivers onto mutually perpendicular directions called components. It does this by finding the first component direction so that a maximum of the variation is explained. Then it finds the component that explains the next-most variation that is left. And so on, till there is a component for each driver. This works because it’s a theorem in linear algebra math that we can do it. If the drivers are multicollinear to some degree, some of the components won’t make much improvement. But there will probably be some number of components that will produce a good enough explanation of the variation. We could then have a linear model using just these few components, reducing the dimensionality of the problem (with some loss, of course).

One common question is whether the components have any meaning. Or have we just confused the user with some synthetic numbers not tied to any reality? The answer is yes and no. You may be able to interpret the components in some human knowledge terms, by examining exactly how they are made up from the drivers. These are called loadings.

Let us try to reduce the dimensionality by finding principal components. We must install the pls library first; don’t forget.

There is randomness involved because we are going to use 10-fold cross-validation, the default for the CV method. We did not do cross-validation on the linear regression above. Let’s set the seed so results will be reproducible.

set.seed(2)

As the book indicates, scaling variables is desirable so one large variable doesn’t overly influence outcome; the CV validation is done by cross validation; we use the parameter scale=TRUE.

Run on all the data. This version of PCA is good because it does the crossvalidation as it calculates the PCs.

pcr.fit=pcr(Salary~., data=Hitters, scale=TRUE, validation ="CV")
summary(pcr.fit)

We see that 19 components were considered, and results were obtained for everything from a single component to all 19 components.

The cross-validation score is provided for each possible number of components, ranging from M = 0 onwards. Note that pcr() reports the root mean squared error (RMSE).

The bottom TRAINING section shows us the percentage of variation of Salary that is explained by that number of components. We can see that the numbers increase, which we would expect. But how much of the gain is significant?

One can also plot the cross-validation scores using the pcr::validationplot() function. Using val.type="RMSEP" will cause the cross-validation RMSE to be plotted.

validationplot(pcr.fit ,val.type="RMSEP", type="b")

This plot is easily reproduced with ggplot by extracting the components and RMSE values using function RMSEP().

d = data.frame(comps = RMSEP(pcr.fit)$comps, val = RMSEP(pcr.fit)$val["CV",,])
ggplot(d) +
  geom_point(aes(comps, val), shape=2, color="red")+
  geom_line(aes(comps, val), linetype="dashed" )+
  theme_bw()

From the plot we also see that the cross-validation error is roughly the same when only one component is included in the model. This suggests that a model that uses just a small number of components might suffice. We could pick say 2 components. The next minimum seems to be at 6 components.

The summary() function also provides the percentage of variance explained in the predictors and in the response using different numbers of components. This concept is discussed in greater detail in Chapter 10. Briefly, we can think of this as the amount of information about the predictors or the response that is captured using M principal components. For example, setting M = 1 only captures 38.31% of all the variance, or information, in the predictors. We get 60% with M=2. In contrast, using M = 6 increases the value to 88.63%.

Visualizing PCR results

One way to visualize the principal components is to plot them in a biplot(). These are for just components 1 and 2. These are equivalent. Notice how the rownames, the player names, appear in the plot.

biplot(pcr.fit, comps=c(1,2))

plot(pcr.fit, comps=c(1,2), plottype = "biplot")

You can also plot the factor loadings.

biplot(pcr.fit, comps=c(1,2), which = "loadings")

loadingplot(pcr.fit, comps=1:2, scatter=T, labels="names")

This could be helpful in trying to explain the PCA model. The first two components are shown on the graph axes. The position of a driver name shows what it contributes to the component. You can see that current AtBats, Hits, RBI, HmRun and Walks contribute a lot to both components. However, Years and Career drivers contribute a lot to component 1 and negatively to component 2.

And Errors, Assists and PutOuts contribute most to component 2 and little or nothing to component 1. The league and division factors contribute negatively to component 2 and also negatively to component 1.

So can we say that component 1 is hitting and component 2 is league and fielding? It makes some sense. How useful is this anthropomorphism of the data?

Read Chapter 10.2.1 about Principal Components ISLR (2013) to learn what all this means. Note that the principal components are normalized and orthogonal (a fancy term for uncorrelated, or perpendicular, in n-dimensional space of course).

We do not use fancy visualizations in this notebook because the factoextra package does not handle objects made by the pcr package.

Predictions

We can get an idea of the RMSE of the PCA model using three components. The caret and yardstick packages each contain functions for computing RMSE and other performance measures. the latter is tidyverse-compatible and probably should be used.

pred=pcr.fit$fitted.values[,1,3]
M = tibble(pred, est=Hitters$Salary)
M %>% yardstick::rmse(est, pred)

A predplot plots the predicted values of Salary against the measured values. The red line shows what the values would be if there were perfect prediction. Clearly the prediction with 3 components is not perfect.

predplot(pcr.fit, ncomp=3, ylim=c(0, 2500))
abline(0,1, col="red")

# We prefer this way.
ggplot() +
  geom_point(aes(Hitters$Salary,pcr.fit$fitted.values[,1,3]))+
  coord_cartesian(ylim=c(0,2500))+
  geom_abline(aes(slope=1, intercept=0), color="red")+
  labs(title="Salary, 3 components, validation",
       x="Measured", y="Predicted")

The high priced players measured are not as valuable as their pay would indicate.

A Neural Net for Comparison

We can use the neuralnet package to engage in dimension reduction as well. But the dimensions will be hidden. We have to scale the numeric drivers. We use two layers, containing 6 and 3 neuron nodes respectively, in the two layers.

It takes a while to run. One of the issues with AI is the long run times. We can make a plot of the result:

plot(nn.fit)

You can see the hidden layers of derived variables, resulting finally in 3 features which might be like components. The final estimates of Salary are done using the last 3 features.

The predictions are given by

nn.pred=predict(nn.fit, newdata=hitters.nn)
nn.pred %>% length
[1] 263

Since they are scaled we need to change them to unscaled values by adding the mean of Salary and the result multiplied by the standard deviation of Salary. We can also compute the RMSE of the nn approximation.

nn.Salary = mean(Hitters$Salary) + sd(Hitters$Salary)*nn.pred
rmse_vec(Hitters$Salary, nn.Salary %>% as.numeric())
[1] 79.93125
ggplot() +
  geom_point(aes(Hitters$Salary, nn.Salary)) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim=c(0,2500)) +
  geom_abline(aes(slope=1, intercept=0), color="red") +
  labs(title="Neural Network with (4,3) nodes, Salary",
       x="Measured", y="Predicted")

The neural network seems to have “over-fit” the data, matching the actual salaries too closely and not leaving any room for finding discrepancies. That’s because it is using nonlinear fitting and randomness with sampling of many trials to build the features. A neural network does not seem to be a good model for baseball salaries, for the purpose of working out who is underpaid and who is overpaid. The general manager’s goal cannot be met by this model.

PCA with FactoMineR package

?`FactoMineR-package`

First identify the qualitative variables.

# find column numbers of factors
H = Hitters %>% select(-Salary)
# H %>% skim
# H %>% names
H %>% select(-where(is.numeric)) %>% names
[1] "League"    "Division"  "NewLeague"
quali = match(H %>% select(-where(is.numeric)) %>% names,
      H %>% names)
quali
[1] 14 15 19

Use FactoMineR package PCA.

# 
G = H %>% PCA(quali.sup=quali)

Conclusion

We followed the article by Michy (2016) to apply principal components analysis to the Hitters data. We used the pcr package for the fit, which does 10-fold crossvalidation automatically. We obtained the principal components, and found that just two components captured about 60% of the variation in the data.

We also compared the predictions to a neural network model. The neural network ‘overfit’ the data; While it got lower RMSE, it did not reveal the overpaid and underpaid players as well.

Finally, we explored the FactoMineR and factoextra packages, an alternate way to do PCA and other multivariate data analyses.
